details:
The GALiverse A.R.E.S. project is a comprehensive Mars analog site selection and simulation platform that evaluates two major volcanic regions in Türkiye: the Meke Lake and Karapınar Volcanic Area, and Divlit Volcanic Park within the Kula-Salihli UNESCO Global Geopark, using space-science-inspired assessment criteria.

At the core of the project is the M.A.F.I. (Mars Analog Fidelity Index) hybrid model, which evaluates eight Mars analog assessment criteria on a scale of 0 to 10. The resulting 80-point raw score, calculated by assigning equal weights to all eight criteria, is normalized to a 100-point scale. Rather than assigning each site a single general score, the system separates the assessment into two specialized branches: the Astrobiology and Aqueous Processes Sub-index and the Engineering, Mobility, and Underground Habitat Sub-index. This approach enables a comparative assessment of which site is more suitable for specific mission objectives. The Python-based simulation architecture integrates these results with orbital and topographic datasets to model terrain-informed rover routes and potential habitat locations.

The project aims to establish a quantitative evaluation framework that reduces subjectivity in Mars analog site selection. It combines Karapınar's potential for astrobiological and aqueous-process research with Divlit's engineering-related advantages, including its volcanic terrain and potential lava tube environments, within a unified assessment framework. By matching instruments and technologies with the most appropriate terrestrial testing environments before actual Mars missions, the project seeks to support cost and time optimization. Its broader objective is to increase the international scientific visibility of Türkiye's unique geological heritage as a potential destination for high-fidelity Mars analog research. Additionally, the project aims to develop an open-source framework integrating artificial intelligence, satellite imagery, and geophysical data for high-school researchers and science clubs.

Python was used as the primary programming language, with Pandas and Matplotlib supporting numerical modeling and data visualization. Microsoft Planetary Computer provided elevation and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data. NASA Mars Trek and its mapping services were used for Martian orbital and cartographic data, while ESA's Global Map of Hydrated Minerals provided hydrated mineral datasets. Thermal spectrometer data were obtained from the Arizona State University's Mars Space Flight Facility archives. Anthropic's Claude and NVIDIA's Nemotron-3 Ultra were used as supporting tools during simulation architecture development and coding, while Google Gemini assisted with literature review and methodological synthesis. Canva was used for visual design and presentation.

The innovative aspect of this project lies in its original hybrid assessment framework, which brings astrobiological potential and rover engineering considerations together within a unified mathematical model and applies it to real planetary and terrestrial datasets. Throughout the development process, the team prioritized scientific integrity by acknowledging environmental differences between Earth and Mars, including differences in gravitational and atmospheric conditions, rather than overlooking their effects. These limitations were reflected in the assessment of environmental extremes. Furthermore, geological characteristics, terrain accessibility, rover mobility risks, and potential habitat suitability were considered together. The results were also supported by vector-based visualizations to improve clarity and facilitate evaluation by the jury.
